How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast.** The judge is `Specification/`, the Working Draft of February 2011 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it (P-25). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states the revival's changes (P-95). The floor to measure against is a pure-Java microGPT, not yet written (PLAN phase 6).
- P-8 **Where the designers left no word, he decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** He accepts the language's unfinished corners rather than stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the type papers or the library, and takes the designers to have known more than he does. So a review checks his decisions against their intent, for errors of commission and of omission; its items are decisions in this file. Detail: `reviews/decisions-review/judgement.md`, "In short".
- P-9 **The search is for microGPT's most readable expression.** In his words, "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." The two sources are Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation, with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms. The flat program in Hsu's style, C4, fell short, so polishing happens in the vocabulary, the operations the model is written in. C4 is the APL program's target form. Its hyperparameters are tuple bindings, the form an APL strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form of those lines is set aside.
- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its remaining ground, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, is not pursued.** Its sub-language expands APL to Fortress code over native arrays, and its APL microGPT program stays in the walk check (P-30).
- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless he asks.** Fortify's mathematical rendering bakes one view of a computation into the syntax, though the same mathematics can be written many ways. APL's one glyph for each transformation does that better. It is presentation only, off the path, and no argument for Fortress.
- P-12 **The type checker on interpreter programs comes after the switch-over.** He wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs, and sees it as low-hanging fruit. Today it checks only against the compiler's prelude (F-9). It comes once walk also takes the static coercions that the checker inserts (P-59).

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- P-16 **He reads the project's end as the price of doing no work on performance.** DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into its third phase in 2006, and the project went on at Sun Labs until 2012. The team worked on syntax, and the compiler that was to make the mathematical types fast never came; the funding was cut for good reason.
- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main cost on microGPT's array kernels (F-11). Boxing is measured on microGPT-shaped kernels, not on a scalar loop with literals and a `:=` accumulator, which microGPT never runs. The storage is P-84's decision; unboxed arithmetic is PLAN phase 6 (P-33).
- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted on its history.** The files that still say so wait for the lineage cleanup (PLAN, "Off the path, parked"), which `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists. His plan to make the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch `main` is not carried out (F-165).

## Decisions on record

### The standard and the sources

- P-25 **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished 2012 restart (F-166) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, it is their latest intent, which the goal is to finish. It covers the exclusion rule, as instantiation exclusion in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, and `Bottom`, which no program can write.
- P-26 **The type group's late positions outweigh the specification's early text where they conflict.** The early text was a wish. The type group then made the language run, for performance and with specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. So their later word wins: the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiler prelude's tower flattened in 2009 and 2010 (P-43), Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper. The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.
- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Next is the algebraic layer: `Ring`, `Field` and what the matrices and tensors of machine learning need, so that the library's traits reach them. It goes into the standard library itself (P-27), not into a tree of the revival's own.
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is hundreds of times slower than Python's interpreter. So no performance decision of any kind, and no edit of C4, the flat model program, for speed, until microGPT runs compiled. The gate never runs the two microGPT programs, too long-running to be tests: it compiles them and records the phase that each reaches. A run of them, once possible, goes to a stage that does not gate.
- P-30 **The microGPT walk check after a batch runs in under a minute.** It runs about two forward-and-backward passes against the reference values, which shows that the model's mathematics still works and that the library's changes did not break it. The full check programs run only when asked. A slower check is to him a waste of time.
- P-32 **The territory map (`coordinator/map/`) maps the tree down to where the design intent is written, in the papers as well as the specification.** It exists so that nothing on record is found again from scratch.

trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

What a commit did:
  created          a text new in POSITIONS.md that no removed or earlier text explains
  changed          a text that replaced another of the same commit (link: number, line, title or similarity)
  moved to history the text left POSITIONS.md and stands verbatim in POSITIONS-history.md
=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

You're close. Three corrections, then why `Any` isn't just the status quo.

**`Any` and `Bottom` are opposite ends.**
- `Any` is the top: every type sits below it, and every value in Fortress belongs to it.
- `Bottom` is the bottom: it sits below every type and has no values at all. It's the type of an expression that never returns a value, such as `throw`.
- The question in item 3 is only about the top. When a generic declaration writes `[\T\]` with no bound, what may `T` be?

**What `Object` is in Fortress.** It isn't Scala's `object` keyword, although Fortress has a similar keyword:
- A Fortress `object` declaration makes values. Without parameters it's a singleton, like Scala's `object`. With parameters, like `object Just[\T\](x: T)`, it's a constructor, much like a Scala case class. So your memory connects the right things.
- The type `Object` is the supertype of every value those declarations make.
- There are no Java-style primitives at the language level. `ZZ32`, `RR64` and `String` are all under `Object`. The unboxed `double` is only how the compiler may store an `RR64`.

**What `Any` has that `Object` doesn't:** tuples like `(ZZ32, ZZ32)`, functions like `ZZ32 -> ZZ32`, and the empty tuple `()`. In Fortress these are not objects. The 2012 Types chapter says the same: `Any` is the top, and `Object` excludes function types.

**Why `Any` isn't just the status quo:**
- The library's own design needs it. A two-dimensional array is indexed by a pair: `Array[\RR64, (ZZ32, ZZ32)\]`. A list of pairs is `List[\(K, V)\]`. Under `Object`, every generic container instantiated at a tuple would be refused. That was measured at 163 refusals, most of them tuple index types, including the arrays microGPT uses.
- The draft's sentence saying `Object` dates from 2008 to 2010, before the library instantiated generics at tuples everywhere. The 2012 Types chapter makes `Any` the top.
- The compile path currently writes `Object` for an empty bound (row 412), which is why it refuses generics at tuple types today. That divergence goes away at the switch-over.

So the choice is between the draft's 2008 wording and what the library needs and the designers' later text says. Option 1 writes `Any` into the specification with a callout recording that the draft said `Object`.

"""tlib: the curator's messages, and the coordinating session's message that each one answered,
read along the transcript's reply chain (standard library).

His messages are exactly what explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/show.py's load() gives: the
live transcripts, the backup copies in /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded (the .parts folders
and the copy until 2026-10-08T15-41 included) and the first session on the `transcripts` branch;
deduplicated by uuid; queued messages with the time he sent them. load_msgs() rebuilds that list
from a per-file index (cache below) with show.py's own functions, in show.py's file order, so the
list is the same; tests.py checks it against show.load().

The message he answered (Talk.answered) follows the chain of the transcript itself: each line's
parentUuid (a compaction's logicalParentUuid), back from his message. Every line on the chain is
one of:
  his     a message of his (show.py's test), or his message queued while a turn ran, delivered
          into that turn (a queued_command attachment that is not a notification)
  text    an assistant line of the session (not a sidechain) holding text
  note    a prompt that is not his: Stop-hook feedback, an agent's message or hand-back, a task
          notification (also a scheduled check-in), a system reminder, a prompt starting '<'
  pass    everything else, passed through: tool calls and results, attachments, hook summaries,
          and the prompts that only continue a turn (a compaction summary, "Continue from where
          you left off", a worker restart notice, a skill's text, an image, a local command)
Going back from his message, the texts met are collected; reaching a note drops them as a turn
not to him (they are listed as skipped), and reaching a prompt of his makes them the answer: the
coordinator's whole turn after that prompt, every text of it, oldest first. A text written after
he sent his message (a queued message is delivered late) is listed apart, not taken. The turns to
him further back on the chain are kept too (Talk.answered(..., earlier=3)), for a reply to an
older question. Two checks on the rule: a skipped turn that answers a notification and ends with
an ask to him (ASK: a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend", "your yes", ...) is marked 'asks',
since the coordinator often relays an agent's result with a question; and when his message
quotes lines ("> ..."), the newest text on the chain that holds them is found ('quoted').
Talk.reply(m) gives the coordinator's turn after his message m.

Cache: ./cache/tx3-<path hash>.pickle, one per transcript file, holding the file's index and its

**Ring, Field, and the `RR64` finding.** These are names for what a set of values can do. An additive group: you can add, subtract, and there is a zero. A ring: an additive group where you can also multiply, with a one. A field: a ring where you can also divide by anything but zero. Integers form a ring, reals form a field, matrices of a given size form a ring but not a field. The point of the traits is that once a type declares which of these it is, everything written in terms of the operations comes for free. The finding: the specification's array chapter writes its element bound as `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]`, and the shipped `RR64` is not declared to satisfy it, so a function written the spec's way refuses real numbers (probe `v04b_groupbound.out.0`); the bound that works is `T extends Number`, which is not algebra but a name. That is the first thing to fix in the layer you want. It is now in `FACTS.md`.

**"Fleshing out the standard library."** Recorded as your position. One question only you can answer, and I have not assumed the answer: the standing rule is that `Library/` is never modified, and this direction reads as modifying it. The alternative is building the algebraic layer in our own tree, over the shipped traits, which is what every run so far has done. Worklist item 4 is literally "unseal the linear-algebra layer", five rows. Say which.

**The checker in the interpreter.** It is not on the ledger as a fix, and neither of us missed a row: the nearest is row 69, which records that `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude and so is not an oracle for interpreter programs. Making the checker usable on interpreter programs means giving it the interpreter's prelude, which falls under worklist item 2 and was never named on its own. It is named now, in `FACTS.md` and `POSITIONS.md`.

**Performance.** Recorded as your priority in `POSITIONS.md`, in your words. Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.

An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.

## What walk checks

Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It refuses:

- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it loads the pair only if the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the return-type rule hold on their declared domains, except in the cases that `revival-changes.md` lists. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes, so such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail. `revival-changes.md`, "Walk's check of two generic declarations", defines the declared domain and lists those cases.
- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`) in a type that provides both.
- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.

POSITIONS-history.md:820:- P-76 **The numeral switch, split by where the static types are.** A numeral has a type of its own, `IntLiteral`, that each number type converts from, the compiler library's 
The warning's consequence, R8's question, is measured: under the switch `3 + 4` is `7 : IntLiteral` and `2147483647 + 1` is `2147483648 : IntLiteral`, no overflow (`PROBE-Q.md` section 5). Arithmetic among bare numerals stays on numerals, exact and unbounded, and lands on a number type at the first typed binding, parameter or operand. That is the specification's intent, not a defect, and microGPT's values do not move. The library's own numeral sites hold: the two strides sum as before, `0 MAX (index - 1)` answers `ZZ32`, the empty sums answer at their types.

So nothing in probe Q argues against the decision. What it shows is where walk cannot follow it yet.

### 4.2 The walk half meets the limit Pavol already accepted on 2026-09-29

R7 (POSITIONS 2026-09-29, walk's run-time choice of coercions): walk has no static types, so it chooses a coercion on the value where the compiled path resolves it statically; accepted as the interpreter's limit, "one now and two after the switch", walk to be matched once the checker runs on interpreter programs after the switch-over and walk takes the static coercions the checker inserts.
The second group of section 3 is the same limit under another name. `<|1, 2, 3|>` at a `List[\ZZ32\]` parameter is typed by the checker from the parameter; walk builds it from the values and gets `List[\IntLiteral\]`. `getDefault(0, 0, 0)` at an instance walk built from `ZZ32` values gets `(Int, Int, Int)`, into which a numeral does not convert. When walk takes the checker's static arguments and coercions, each of these is settled by the same insertion R7 waits for, with nothing built for it in walk. Building it now, as option 1 asks (row 364's repair beside the devices), writes into walk's inference from values an approximation of static typing that the switch-over then replaces, and by the probe's own reading still does not match the checker. That is work the goal does not need: microGPT's values are unchanged under the switch, its static types are concrete, and rows 79, 443, 454 and 4

So the walk half of rung Q waits, for the same reason and to the same point as R7's second step. This keeps the decision (walk switches to `IntLiteral`) and moves its date, on evidence he did not have on 2026-09-27.

### 4.3 The library half does not need to wait, and should not

The one library's `IntLiteral` model is what the compiled path needs at the switch-over: when the compiler's prelude is deleted and its tests kept (PLAN phase 4), tests that rely on a numeral's own type (`typecase` answering `other`, `litCoercion`, `NumeralTest`) keep their verdicts only if the one library carries the sibling. On the checker the model costs nothing once `ZZ32` states its four comparisons on itself: 623 against the landed 627, the four fewer being the old `IntLiteral`'s two getter errors and the stage's run-to-run variation (section 2). It closes row 454's integer half on the checker's side (the one library accepts `a: NN32 = 3`) and gives the checker the model rung I's numeral tie rule assumes.
### 4.4 What goes into each half

**The library rung (call it Q-lib), in batch 8.** Library and glue only, no evaluator file.
- The compiler library's `IntLiteral` as a sibling under `Number`: `object IntLiteral extends Number`, `Number`'s comprises clause taking it, `ZZ32`'s giving it up, the getters `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64`, `asZZ` over five natives in `glue/prim/IntLiteral.java` (38 lines of the shadow), the team's arithmetic block enabled with its warning quoted in the rung's record (R8), `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` (`lib-switch.patch`, 225 lines). As an object, `IntLiteral` excludes `QQ` under walk (row 484's condition) and `XXXextendIntLiteral` stays an expected failure.
- Kind A's device: `AnyIntegral`'s `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` (`lib-r.patch`), or the per-type overloads; the rung lists both and takes the smaller unless it finds a reason.
- `ZZ32`'s `>`, `>=`, `<=` and `CMP` on `ZZ32` itself, as `ZZ64` states them (`lib-r1.patch`, 30 lines), and item 33's two halves under decision 2's device: `CMP` on each integer type that lacks it, and the ten `MAXNUM`/`MINNUM` declarations (row 517, which exists on the base, `XXXIntegerMaxNumRungM` promoted).
- The numeral case in `exactValue`: one `typecase` arm, `z: IntLiteral => Ratio(z.asZZ, 1)` or the getter's equivalent (`lib-eq1.patch`, 10 lines), so that `Number`'s `=` never reaches `Ratio(0, 0)` for a numeral. Correct and the library's own device; its cost (section 4.5) is not paid while walk's numeral is an `Int`.
The record put batch 7b after batch N because 7b's rung W and N's walk rung share `OverloadedFunction.java` (PLAN, phase 3, item 5). With Q-walk moved past the switch-over, that reason is gone: Q-lib touches no evaluator file, and W's files are `OverloadedFunction.java`, `FGenericFunction.java`, `GenericFunctionOrMethod.java`, `GenericConstructor.java` and, under the decided items, `MakeInferenceSpecific.java` and `types/FType.java` (`CLIMB-BATCH-7.md`, rung W, "Files it may touch"). So the order becomes: batch 6.5b lands (gathering now); batch 7b; batch 8 with Q-lib in its library work beside R9; the checker at a true zero; the switch-over; Q-walk as a rung of the batch that gives walk the checker's static types, or the one after. Batch N's second run as recorded is retired, and its record's section 1 says so in one paragraph; rows 79, 443, 437's walk half and 486 move to Q-walk's line 

### 4.8 What could go wrong

- The switch-over's "walk takes the checker's static types" step is R7's plan and is not designed. If it is cut, or comes late, Q-walk needs option 1's full set at that time. The cost then is option 1's cost now, and nothing built meanwhile is lost: Q-lib is needed under every shape.
- Q-lib's expected zero change to walk's outputs rests on the reading that no `IntLiteral` value reaches the library under walk save a numeral below -2^63. The rung's comparison over the 440 tests is the check; a changed output is listed, and a numeral below -2^63 in a test would be the first place to look.
- Row 432 (`SUM <|1, 2, 3|>`) stays open under both halves: the probe found it refused under the switch too, over `ArrayList[\IntLiteral\]`, because `IntLiteral` carries no additive algebra. Whether Q-lib gives `IntLiteral` the algebra every flat number type carries is the rung's choice to list, not this judgement's; the row is not on microGPT's path.

--- text 2026-09-08T21:07:05.628Z  origin/transcripts:projects/-home-user-fortress/bdff267d-67dc-5bb9-b970-8c3dfaa634b6.jsonl.parts/001.jsonl:2530  (2403 characters)
Yes, largely a soft problem, and Scala is the right place to copy from, with one adjustment.

**Scala's `for` is the same trick.** A `for` comprehension desugars into `foreach`, `map`, `flatMap` calls with a closure per body, exactly as Fortress desugars `for` and `Σ` into `generate` calls with a closure. Scala did not solve the cost with a new idea. It used three known ones:

1. **Let the JIT inline.** When a closure call site sees one closure class, HotSpot inlines it and the loop body becomes a plain loop. `Range.foreach` is written as a `while` loop over an `Int`, so once the closure inlines, the JIT sees a counted loop and does its bounds-check elimination and vectorization.
2. **Inline at compile time when the JIT cannot.** The Scala 2.12 optimizer inlines closures and small methods across the standard library; Scala 3 has `inline` as a language feature. This is what removes the closure when the call site is polymorphic.
3. **Specialize the function types**, so that a closure from `Int` to `Double` does not box its argument and result.

All three transfer to Fortress's code generator. Static types from the checker tell it when a call site is monomorphic, and the desugarer already knows which closures it created.

**The adjustment.** Fortress's `generate` is not `foreach`. It is a parallel divide-and-conquer over the generator, with a reduction object supplying the join, forked onto the work-stealing pool. Scala had that too, as the parallel collections, and the lesson there is unflattering: for small bodies the task overhead dominates, and Scala moved them out of the standard library. Java's parallel streams learned the same lesson and split only above a size threshold, running a sequential loop inside each chunk. Our probe showed the same thing: no speedup at four threads on a 16-element vector.

So the Fortress version of the copy is: sequential `while` loops as the default lowering for a range generator, closures inlined by the two mechanisms above, and fork-join only above a size threshold, with the reduction's monoid structure telling the compiler the split is legal. That last part is the one thing Fortress has that Scala lacks: the library declares the algebra, so the compiler does not have to guess whether reordering is safe.

None of this is research. It is a lowering pass plus a library policy, and the Scala optimizer is a worked example to read.

2566 2026-09-08T21:17:58.819Z The roadmap is attached and committed at 7a9f57cea as a proposal, not an approved plan. Your three questions, answered in it and here:  **Both routes is not too ambitious, if sequenced.** They share the front end and a Phase 0, and they touch disjoint code: Route A edits the code generator and compiler library, Route B adds a new evaluator package. Same golden gate and benchmark table, so the comparison is fair by construction. The economics differ. Route A is incremental and worker-sized. Route B has a long silent period before the first program runs end to end and wants one worker holding the whole evaluator. So: start A's first steps as parallel workers, start B as one long-running worker, and hold a checkpoint when either runs the microGPT forward pass.  **Type checking in the interpreter.** No version of the interpreter does it today. The phase list for `walk` includes the checker, but the shell switches it off and there is no command-line flag to turn it on. Enabling it is Phase 0.1: add the switch, run the 2012 prelude through the checker for the first time, and catalogue what breaks. The team's own 43 not-working static tests are the starting list.  **Is type resolution necessary for Truffle?** Not strictly. Truffle specializes on the types it observes at run time. But static types make the first guesses right and the guards cheap, and they are the only way the interpreter becomes spec-conforming. For Route A they are mandatory, since every Scala technique starts from a known static type. So Phase 0.1 sits on the critical path of both.
----
2602 2026-09-08T21:22:33.094Z Reflowed and resent. Both the roadmap and the backend notes now have one line per paragraph and a blank line between every numbered item, committed at 883ec948c and pushed. I will write documents that way from here on.
----
2609 2026-09-08T21:26:27.316Z Take one line from the blinded run's program:  ```fortress opr juxtaposition(W: Mat, x: Vec): Vec = ...    (* matrix times vector *) opr juxtaposition(a: Vec, M: Mat): Vec = ...    (* row vector times matrix *) ```  Two definitions of the same operator, distinguished only by the types of their two arguments. When the program later writes `alpha Vh`, something has to pick one. How that pick is made is the whole story.  **How Java picks.** At compile time, from the declared types of the arguments, the compiler chooses one overload and writes its exact name into the bytecode. At run time the only choice left is virtual dispatch: which class's version of that one method to run, decided by the run-time class of the receiver alone, the object before the dot. The other arguments have no say. That is single dispatch, and it is what the JVM's `invokevirtual` instruction does natively.  **How Fortress picks.** The specification says the applicable definition is chosen by the run-time types of all the arguments, and the most specific applicable one wins. No argument is privileged, hence "symmetric". `self` in a method is just the first argument. The two juxtapositions above, `opr +(self, other: Value)` beside `opr +(self, other: RR64)`, and every other overload in the language are resolved this way. Because every function and operator in Fortress is overloadable, this is the calling convention for every call, not a special feature used occasionally.  **What that forces.** Three things:  1. Every value must carry its full run-time type, including generic instantiation, because `f(xs: List[\Value\])` and `f(xs: List[\RR64\])` are different overloads that the dispatcher must tell apart. Java's erased generics make that impossible, which is why the 2012 compiler generates instantiated classes at load time. 2. The set of overloads must be provably unambiguous for every possible combination of run-time types, not only the ones the compiler sees. That is the meet rule and the return-type rule from `Papers/Dispatch`, checked statically. Those rules are the price of symmetry. 3. At each call, some code must look at the types of the arguments and choose. The 2012 compiler's overload-rewriting phase generates, for every overloaded name, one dispatch function that tests argument types from most to least specific and then calls the chosen body. Every call goes through it, even `alpha Vh`, where the static types already decided the answer. The JIT sees a type-test chain and an ind
----
2626 2026-09-08T21:27:20.757Z Start from what Java does, because the Fortress mechanism is a reaction to it.  **Java erases.** `List<Double>` and `List<String>` are one class at run time, `List`. The compiler checks the type arguments and then throws them away. That is cheap and it is why Java generics were retrofittable in 2004, but it means no run-time code can ask a list what its element type is.  **Fortress cannot erase**, for the reason in the previous answer: dispatch must tell `List[\Value\]` from `List[\RR64\]` at run time, and the spec says types are never erased. So every instantiation of a generic trait, object, or function has to exist as its own run-time entity with its own name.  **How the 2012 compiler does it.** The code generator compiles a generic declaration such as `object Box[\T\](v: T)` once, into a *template* classfile in which the type parameter `T` is left as a placeholder inside names and method descriptors. It does not produce `Box` of anything. Then, at run time, a custom class loader in `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java` does the rest:  1. Some code asks the JVM for a class whose name carries the instantiation, spelled with Unicode oxford brackets, for example `Box⟦RR64⟧`. That name is how the compiler encodes "Box instantiated at RR64". `Naming.java` defines the bracket characters and the mangling rules. 2. The class loader parses the name, finds the template `Box`, and reads its bytes. 3. It runs the template through an ASM bytecode rewriter that substitutes the concrete types for the placeholders: class names, field types, method signatures, the interfaces it implements, the calls it makes to other generics, which in turn get their own bracketed names. 4. It hands the rewritten bytes to `defineClass`, and the JVM now has a real class `Box⟦RR64⟧`, distinct from `Box⟦String⟧`, each loadable and dispatchable.  The same machinery handles generic functions and generic methods, via `MethodInstantiater`, and the RTTI objects in `compiler/runtimeValues/` are what a value carries so that the dispatcher can ask "which instantiation are you".  **What it costs.**  - A class per instantiation, generated by bytecode surgery at load time. Let me pull the facts for the parts that have them in the tree before answering: which algebraic traits ship versus what the specification describes, whether the interpreter's static checker is even on, and what the compiled-path note measured.
=========
10783 2026-09-15T09:51:20.618Z 5350
Definitions first, then the three questions that have hard answers in the tree, then the two you asked me to start. One of the facts below changes the picture on both the type checking and the speed.

## The words

- **Reshape**: take the elements of an array in order and lay them out in a different shape. `(2,3)⍴` of six numbers is a two-by-three matrix. Hsu's layout lives on this: the parameters are one flat vector of 4192 numbers and each weight matrix is a reshape of a slice of it.
- **Ravel** (`,`): the opposite, flatten any array into a vector in row-major order. `⊃,/,¨` in the program ravels nine gradient matrices and joins them into the one flat gradient vector.
- **Planes**: a rank-3 array is a stack of matrices; each matrix in the stack is a plane. The attention block is one plane per (document, head) pair, and `⍤2` means "do this to every plane".
- **Gather**: pick rows of a matrix by a list of indices. `wte[ids;]` takes the embedding row of every token in the batch.
- **Outer product** (`∘.f`): apply `f` to every pair from two vectors, giving a matrix. `ids∘.=⍳27` compares each token id with each of the 27 vocabulary indices, which is the one-hot matrix; `(⍳16)∘.≥⍳16` compares positions and is the causal mask.

## Ring, Field, and which specification

I search the in-repo `Specification/` tree, which is the later draft with the implementers' notes, not the frozen 1.0. On the algebraic library the draft's chapter is `advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex`, and its `Ring` and `Field` declarations are there as commented-out LaTeX, lines 1541 and 1761, never made normative. The shipped library has `AdditiveGroup`, `MultiplicativeRing` and an `AnyMultiplicativeRing` marker, nothing more; and, as the Fable review found, the shipped `RR64` does not even satisfy the spec's `AdditiveGroup` bound. On positional arguments, the same draft: nothing, in any chapter or in the parser.

## The `nat` parameters, and the fact that changes things

You have the intent exactly right, and there are two reasons your expectation is not met here, one of them new.

The first I gave: the specification says `nat` parameters are "instantiated at runtime", so they were never meant as compile-time constants that a code generator folds; the design is dimension checking, not dimension-driven optimization. I know of no paper on this specifically; the published type-system work from the team (the OOPSLA 2011 paper on modular multiple dispatch, in `research/README.md`) is about overloading, not sizes.

The second is in `repo-internals.md` and I should have led with it: the static type checker exists, in Scala, and the walk interpreter never runs it. The `walk` command turns it off, and the phase is a no-op, so the interpreter runs untyped and every "type error" we have ever seen from it is a run-time dispatch failure. The `compile` command turns the checker on. So the compile-time error you are asking about, a mismatched dimension refused before running, is exactly what the compiled path is for, and it is the path this project has characterized but not finished.

That also answers the class-loader question. The bytecode compiler lowers every type to a JVM reference type and emits a dispatch method per overloaded name; there is no place in it where size checks would be generated, because in the design they are the checker's job, ahead of code generation, and the checker is the part that runs only on that path.

## The fast path, and the walking skeleton

The narrow path you describe exists and has numbers. `compiled-path-gaps.md` measured the bytecode compiler against the interpreter on the constructs microGPT is made of: 6.8× on a scalar loop, 8.9× on object allocation and operator calls, numerics identical to the last digit. Its finding is that the gap is not code generation but the compiler's tiny prelude library, with a prioritized worklist. So the skeleton is: take C4's program and vocabulary, which are plain Fortress, push them through `fortress compile`, and close prelude gaps in the order the program hits them, with the interpreter kept as the debugging path and the goldens as the oracle. That gives both the static checker and the speed on the same road. Truffle on Graal would be a rewrite of the interpreter for a JIT it does not have today; it is a different, larger project and not the first step.

## The inventory you asked for

That is the ledger review, and your framing is the right one for it: not "what is broken" but "where does Fortress stand, area by area, against the languages you know, and which of its edges are design, unfinished implementation, or never built". I am launching a Fable worker on that now, over all 287 rows and the ten reports, with your questions as its brief; I review the draft here. It is the document the ordering of the next work should come out of.

On the history: DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three in 2006, and Fortress went on as a Sun Labs project until 2012, so "died for good reasons" is at least half right; the syntax and type machinery are what got built, and the compiler that would have made the parallelism pay is what did not. Hsu's critique lands on that same seam. As for training every model to write APL: the program in `apl/mg/` is nineteen lines and correct to the last bit, so the takeover has a proof of concept.
